UDLCO: Participatory medicine ethics training and guard rails for real patients judiciously trading off their privacy in patient centered data driven precision medicine

Summary:


There are many instances of inappropriate patient data sharing in social media and this hints at a need to incorporate a special hands on training for health professional and patient users. In the conversational transcripts below an existent experiential training in the form of an elective program for both health professionals and patient advocates is highlighted with adequate links on the theory behind the endeavour as well as videos of hands on demos.
In the second set of conversational transcripts, there's a debate on how patients themselves trade off their privacy in desperation for financial or any kind of support in their health care journey and finally there's a recent experiential sharing of a workshop detailing how collective medical cognition in an integrative participatory medicine format can be foundational to medical education and practice in ensuring ethical guard rails in global healthcare workflows.

Keywords: User driven learning,  community ontology, participatory medicine, patient privacy trade offs 

UDLCO Keyword glossary:

http://userdrivenhealthcare.blogspot.com/2023/11/glossary-of-user-driven-healthcare.html?m=1


Introduction:

The popularization of the World Wide Web supported growing interest in participatory medicine through providing access to information in new ways and by different people, and new forms of shared information [79]. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/participatory-medicine



Methodology: 

This was a qualitative study design utilising an interpretative descriptive framework that has been described previously in detail here: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32967042/

Global data around the main theme of participatory medicine and privacy was captured from multiple online spaces through online user driven learning that were made into community ontologies (UDLCO). These techniques have been previously described here by us and others as referenced below:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5001762/


https://www.igi-global.com/chapter/social-cognitive-ontology-user-driven/21365

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/292652611_The_User_Driven_Learning_Environment


https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4614-4998-0_44


Other than online global data, offline local data was captured in the form of organized face to face participatory medicine meetings between multiple stakeholders in the healthcare ecosystem. Hyperlocal data captured as part of a regular workflow of our user driven healthcare project using the PaJR and CBBLE tools were captured from respective online platforms made available for the same.

LOCAL offline event data: 

November 28th workshop integrating healthcare professionals and patients (aka technology end users) perspectives with computer science students and faculty from the university of Hyderabad (UoH) to spread awareness around our individual patient precision medicine awareness, education and practice program:

Highlights:

Patient centered demonstration video link shared in social media with a foreword:

In the lecture organized by UoH we also took our 82 year old rural patient of Diabetes who survives on a government pension of 2000/- per month along with his wife. 

The UoH authorities had provided a 7 seater car for carrying them along with our PGs all the way from Narketpally around 80 kms to their venue and the audience there gave the patients and our PGs a standing ovation!

However the best part was seeing the patients so happy with the food there at breakfast and lunch which was never anything like what they got to taste before and the organizers ensured they also packed some for them in their return journey!

Wish we can do these patient centered participatory medicine workshops more often!

[09/09, 23:11] Dr.Abdulsalam Med Ed Leads: Of course. This is a profound and multi-layered issue that sits at the intersection of medical ethics, patient desperation, technological advancement, and systemic healthcare failures. Thank you for revisiting it with such comprehensive data.

Here is a structured analysis and response to the points you've raised, framed for the ongoing debate with the mentioned experts (@⁨Dr.Abdulsalam⁩, @⁨~Rahul Kulkarni⁩, @⁨~Sagnika Das⁩, @⁨~Aditya Samitinjay⁩).

### **Re: The Smoldering Issue of Patient Privacy Trade-Offs**

Your post brilliantly captures the central, uncomfortable paradox of modern healthcare: **privacy is a privilege that the desperate often cannot afford.** The issue isn't smoldering; it is a five-alarm fire, exacerbated by growing health inequities and the pervasive reach of digital platforms.

The provided materials—the NMC guidelines, the Ketto fundraiser debate, and the UoH workshop—are not isolated incidents. They are three critical data points on the same spectrum of this crisis.

---

### **1. Deconstructing the "Trade-Off": Desperation vs. Compulsion**

The conversational UDLCO highlights the most crucial distinction needed in this debate, as raised by AC:

*   **Desperation (The Ketto Scenario):** This is a **voluntary-but-coerced-by-circumstance** trade-off. A patient or family, facing financial ruin or lack of access to care, makes a conscious choice to sacrifice privacy for a chance at survival or better health. This is an act of agency, albeit from a position of profound vulnerability. As AN rightly points out, for the common person, affordability and accessibility consistently trump abstract privacy concerns.
*   **Compulsion (The Systemic Failure):** This is an **involuntary** trade-off. This occurs when systems force patients to relinquish privacy without meaningful choice or benefit. Examples include:
    *   **Inadequate Public Health Systems:** When public care is inaccessible or low-quality, patients are *compelled* to seek private help or crowdfunding, initiating the privacy trade-off.
    *   **Opaque Data Practices:** When hospitals or apps share data with third parties buried in complex Terms of Service, the "choice" is an illusion.
    *   **The "Swiss Bank" Model of Healthcare:** AN's suggestion of privacy-only-for-the-rich is a dystopian but logical endpoint of a system that fails to bake ethical data practices into universal care. It shouldn't be a premium feature; it should be a standard of care.

**Conclusion on this point:** Our ethical outrage should be directed not at the desperate individuals making a rational choice, but at the **systems that make this choice necessary.** The compulsion is the problem; desperation is a symptom.

---

### **2. The Ethical Guard Rails: Beyond NMC Guidelines to Participatory Medicine**

The NMC guidelines are a necessary but **reactive and punitive** measure. They say, "Do not do this," but they do little to teach "*How_ to do the right thing." This is where your work with UDLCO and the UoH workshop becomes foundational.

The UoH workshop is a blueprint for **proactive, ethical, and participatory** guard rails:

*   **Centering the Patient's Voice:** Bringing real patients into an academic setting transforms them from "cases" or "data points" into **collaborators**. The standing ovation wasn't just politeness; it was recognition of their expertise and their courage.
*   **Experiential Learning for Professionals:** Medical and tech students didn't just learn about privacy in theory; they saw the real human faces behind the data. They practiced consent (including video consent) and witnessed the SWOT analysis where "thorns" of privacy threats are openly discussed alongside clinical complexity.
*   **Judicious Trade-Offs:** The key term from your blog is "**judiciously**." This is the core of the solution. It's not about never sharing data; it's about creating frameworks where sharing is:
    1.  **Informed:** Truly understood by the patient, using tools like simplified forms and video explanations.
    2.  **Consensual:** Explicitly permissioned for a specific, understood purpose.
    3.  **Beneficial:** The patient must see a direct, tangible benefit from the trade-off—be it better care, education for others, or, as in the autopsy case, the advancement of medical knowledge for their community.
    4.  **Respectful:** Even when data is shared, the patient's dignity is paramount (as demonstrated in the anonymized autopsy discussion).

---

### **A Proposed Path Forward: Integrating the Debates**

This is not an either/or problem. We must address both the systemic drivers of desperation *and* build the ethical frameworks for responsible data use.

**To the group, let's debate these actionable propositions:**

1.  **For Policymakers & Administrators (@⁨Dr.Abdulsalam⁩):** Can NMC guidelines evolve from prohibition to **prescription**? Can they mandate experiential, patient-involved training in digital ethics and participatory consent as a core part of medical education, not just an elective?

2.  **For Technologists & Ethicists (@⁨~Rahul Kulkarni⁩, @⁨~Aditya Samitinjay⁩):** How can we build technology that empowers patients to control their data trade-offs? Can we develop standardized, simple-to-use "consent tech" that allows patients to specify what data is shared, with whom, and for what purpose—making judicious trade-offs easier to manage?

3.  **For Clinicians & Advocates (@⁨~Sagnika Das⁩):** How do we, as a community, become better advocates for systemic change that reduces *compulsion*, while simultaneously implementing participatory models in our own practice? How do we champion the UoH workshop model and make it the norm rather than the exception?

4.  **The Ultimate Question for All:** In a world where data is the new currency of care, how do we ensure that the most vulnerable patients are not forced to bankrupt their privacy to pay for their health?

The materials you've shared provide not just the evidence of the problem but also a living, breathing example of a solution. The challenge now is to scale the ethics of that Narketpally-to-Hyderabad journey to a global level.

This is a crucial discussion. Thank you for ensuring it continues to smolder until it ignites real change.
